la:adj:primus.html:
prīmus, a, um,
adj. sup. [obsol. prep. pri (prei); whence also prior, priscus; cf.: privus, privo, etc., and v. pro], the first, first (properly only when three or more are referred to. The first, as opp. to the second, is prior; but primus is rarely used for prior,).
In gen.: qui primus vulnus dicitur obligavisse,: primus sentio mala nostra: primus rescisco omnia: Primus porro obnuntio,: verum primum: verum igitur et extremum,: primae litterae,: primus inter homines nobilissimos,: primi ex omnibus philosophis,: primus Graeciae in Thraciam introiit,: primus de mille fuisses,: in primis,among the first, in the foremost ranks,: in primis stetit,: in primis pugnantes,: leonem primus, aut in primis ferire, : utque pedum primis infans vestigia plantis institerat (= ut primum, etc., poet.), : primus post eos quos poëtae tradiderunt movisse aliqua circa rhetoricen Empedocles dicitur (= secundus or proximus ab iis),.—
In partic.
In time or place, first, fore, foremost, the first part; sometimes to be translated, the end, extremity, etc.: in primā provinciā,at the entrance of the province,: digitus,the tip of the finger,: dentes,the front teeth,: ranis prima lingua cohaeret,the end of the tongue,: primā statim nocte,at the beginning of the night,: sol,i. e. the rising sun,: luna,i. e. the new moon,.—With quisque, the first possible, the very first: primo quoque tempore,at the very first opportunity,: primo quoque die,: me tibi primum quidque concedente,: fluit voluptas et prima quaeque avolat,.—Subst.: prīma, ōrum, n., the first part, the beginning: quod bellum, si prima satis prospera fuissent,.—Of the first principles or elements of things, : prima consiliorum (for prima consilia),: a primo, from the beginning, at first: multum improbiores sunt quam a primo credidi,; ; : in illā pro Ctesiphonte oratione submissius a primo: deinde pressius,: suam vim retinere a primo ad extremum,: hoc a primo cogitavit,; Halm ad loc.: id a primo rectissime dicitur, Madv. ad loc.: in primo, in front, before, in the beginning, first: equites in primo late ire jubet,in the van,: qui numerus in primo viget, jacet in extremo,. —
First in rank or station, chief, principal, most excellent, eminent, distinguished, noble (cf.: princeps, primores): evocat ad se Massiliensium quindecim primos,: sui municipii facile primus,: homo,: primis urbis placuisse,: juvenum primi,: est genus hominum, qui esse primos se omnium rerum volunt Nec sunt,: quia sum apud te primus,I am the first in your favor,: primus humani generis,: urbem Italiae primam,: praedium,: suavia prima habere,to give the first place to, think the most of,: otium atque divitiae, quae prima mortales putant,: cura,a chief part,.—Also, most conspicuous, chief, in a bad sense: peccatores, quorum primus ego sum,: primas partes, or primas agere,to play the first part, to occupy the first rank,: primas in causis agebat Hortensius,; : primas dare, to give the first place, ascribe the greatest importance to a thing: actioni primas dedisse Demosthenes dicitur, cum rogaretur, quid in dicendo esset primum: huic secundas, huic tertias,: primas deferre, to transfer the first or principal part: amoris erga me tibi primas defero,i. e. I assign to you the first rank among those who love me,: primas concedere, to yield the first place: si Allienus tibi primas in dicendo partes concesserit,: primas tenere,to play the first part, be the best,: cum primis, and in primis (also written in one word, impri-mis), with or among the first, chiefly, especially, principally, particularly: homo domi suae cum primis locuples,: in primis lautus eques,: oppidum in primis Siciliae clarum,: homo in primis improbissimus,, § 68: vir magnus in primis,: in primis hoc a se animadversum esse dicebat,: in primis nobis sermo de te fuit,: in primis ... dein,first, in the first place,. —Hence, adv., primo and primum; also, ante- and post-class. and very rare, prime and primiter (the form primo is usually limited to that which is strictly first in time; primum in enumerations of contemporary facts, things, or arguments, where the order is at the speaker's choice; cf. Krebs, Antibarb. p. 920 sq.).
prīmō, at first, at the beginning, first, firstly.
In gen.: aedes primo ruere rebamur,: neque credebam primo mihimet Sosiae,; : primo non accredidit,: Themistocles solus primo profectus est,: contemptus est primo a tyrannis,; .—
With dein, deinde, inde, post, postea, mox, denique, nunc: primo Stoicorum more agamus, deinde nostro instituto vagabimur,: primo pecuniae, dein imperii cupido crevit,: primo ... deinde ... tum ... tum,: primo ... deinde,; ; ; : primo abstinentiā utendum: deinde danda, etc.,: primo ... inde, ... hinc,: haec primo paulatim crescere: post, etc.,: dissuadente primo Vercingetorige, post concedente,: primo ... postea ... postremo, etc.,: primo ... mox,: primo ... mox deinde,: primo negitare, denique saepius fatigatus, etc.,: neque illi credebam primo, nunc vero palam est,.—
(Mostly post-Aug. for primum.) With iterum, rursus, secundo: primo ... iterum,: primo ... rursus,: primo ... secundo,.—
prīmum, at first, first, in the first place, in the beginning (class.).
In enumerations, with a foll. deinde, tum: Caesar primum suo, deinde omnium e conspectu remotis equis,: primum ... deinde ... deinde,: primum ... deinde ... tum ... postremo,: primum ... deinde ... praeterea ... postremo,: primum ... tum ... deinde ... post ... tum ... deinde ....,; ; cf.: primum ... secundo loco ... deinde ... tum,; ; ; ; ; ; : primum ... subinde,: primum ... mox,.—
Without other adverbs.
In gen.: quaerenda pecunia primum est,: te Quicumque primum Produxit,; .—
Strengthened with omnium, first of all, : primum omnium ego ipse vigilo,.—
With ut, ubi, simulac, cum.
Ut primum, ubi primum, simul ac primum, cum primum, as soon as ever, as soon as: ut primum potestas data est augendae dignitatis tuae, etc.,: ubi primum potuit, istum reliquit,: simul ac primum niti possunt, etc.,: tum affuerat, cum primum dati sunt judices,.—
Nunc primum, now first, now for the first time (cf.: nunc demum, now at last): post illa nunc primum audio, Quid illo sit factum,.—
With dum (also by Plaut. joined in one word, pri-mumdum), in the first place, first (anteclass.): primum dum, si falso insimulas, etc. Iterum si id verum est, etc.,: omnium primumdum haed aedes jam face occlusae sicut,; ; : primum dum omnium male dictitatur tibi vulgo in sermonibus,.—
With adv. or other expression of time, for the first time: hodie primum ire in ganeum,: quo die primum convocati su mus,.—*
prīmē, es pecially: fabula prime proba, Naev. ap. P.; cf. P.—
prīmĭter, at first, first of all (ante- and post-class.): eripis primiter dapes, Pompon. ap. ; Inscr. (of the beginning of the third century of Christ) Lab. Epigr. Lat. Scop. in Egitto.

la:verb:privo.gloss: to bereave, deprive, rob or strip of something
senses: to bereave, deprive, rob or strip of something
to free, set apart, release, deliver from something, relieve of
la:verb:privo.html:
prīvo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
privus
.
To bereave, deprive, rob, strip of any thing (class.; cf.: orbo, viduo).
With abl.: haec meretrix meum erum ... privavit bonis, luce, honore,: donis privatus sum,: aliquem approbatione,: praepositio in privat verbum eā vi, quam haberet, si in praepositum non fuisset,: aliquem somno,: se oculis,: aliquem vitā,: aliquem communi luce,: patriam aspectu suo,: cibo,: lumine,: fide,.—
With gen. (anteclass.): me cum privares tui, Afran. ap. (Com. Rel. p. 156 Rib.).—
With acc. (ante-class.): quod res vis hunc privari pulcras quas uti solet? Nov. ap. (l. l. p. 224 Rib.).—
To free, release, deliver from any thing; with abl.: aliquem injuriā,: exsilio,: molestiā,: dolore,: dolore,: dominis superbis,: formidine,.—Hence,
prīvantĭa, ĭum, n., privatives, a transl. of the Gr. στερητικά: sunt enim alia contraria, quae privantia licet appellemus Latine, Graece appellantur στερητικά, .—
prīvātus, a, um, P. a.
Apart from the State, peculiar to one's self, of or belonging to an individual, private (opp. publicus or communis; cf. domesticus; class.): nihil privati ac separati agri,: utatur privatis ut suis,: privatus illis census erat brevis, Commune magnum,: vestem mutare privato consensu, opp. publico consilio,: de communi quicquid poterat, ad se in privatam domum sevocabat,: res quae ipsius erant privatae,private property,: privatae feriae vocantur sacrorum propriorum, velut dies natales, Müll.—
Esp., of persons, not in public or official life, private, deprived of office: cum projectis fascibus et deposito imperio, privatus et captus ipse in alienam venisset potestatem,; : vir privatus, a private individual, one who is not a magistrate, or in any public office: privato viro imperium extra ordinem dare,: Bibulus ex iis, qui privati sunt,: privatus an cum potestate,: privati, opp. reges,.—
Of things: aedificia,isolated, apart from the villages,: vita privata et quieta,a private life, withdrawn from State affairs,.—
Neutr. absol. in the phrases in privato, in private, opp. in publico, in public, : in privatum, for private use: tabernas vendidit in privatum,: ex privato, from one's private property: tributum ex privato conferre,.—
Subst.: prīvātus, i, m. (sc. homo), a man in private life, citizen (opp. magistratus): hic qualis imperator nunc privatus est,: an vero P. Scipio pontifex maximus Ti. Gracchum privatus interfecit; Catilinam nos consules perferemus?.—Plur., : consilium dedimus Sullae, privatus ut altum Dormiret,.—
In the time of the emperors, private, i. e. not imperial, not belonging to the emperor or to the imperial family: id sibi (Domitiano) maxime formidolosum, privati hominis (i. e. Agricolae) nomen supra principis attolli,: ut summum fastigium privati hominis impleret, cum principis noluisset,: spectacula,not given by the emperor,.—Adv.: prīvā-tō, at home (very rare for the class. privatim, q. v.): privato nos tenuissemus, Liv. Fragm. ap. P.

prīvĭlēgĭum, ii, n.
privus-lex
,
a bill or law in favor of or against an individual (class.): in privatos homines leges ferri noluerunt; id est enim privilegium,; cf. ; : de te privilegium tulit,; : licuit tibi ferre non legem, sed nefarium privilegium,: privilegia irrogare,: vim et crudelitatem privilegii publicis litteris consignavit,.—

(110): quaedam privilegia parentibus data sunt, : privilegio munitus,: privilegium aetatis,; , Serm. 13, 15: sacerdotum,: athletarum,.

la:adj:prior.gloss: former, prior, previous, earlier (preceding in time)
senses: former, prior, previous, earlier (preceding in time)
la:adj:prior.html:
prĭor and prĭus (old form also in
neutr. prior, Val. Antias and Quadrig. ap. ), ōris, adj. comp. [from obsol. prep. pri; v. primus init.], former, previous, prior, freq. to be translated first; cf. superior; Cicero nearly always uses prior, opp. to posterior, in time; superior in sense of former, in gen. relation to the present, when no other time is expressed; v. Krebs, Antibarb. p. 921 sq.
Lit.: ita priori posterius, posteriori superius non jungitur,: me quaestorem in primis, aedilem priorem, praetorem primum populus Romanus faciebat,: qui prior has angustias occupaverit,first,: prior proelio lacessere,: etsi utrique primas, priores tamen libenter deferunt Laelio,: priore loco causam dicere,first,: priore aestate,in the former summer, last summer,: priore nocte,: factum est enim meā culpā, ut priore anno non succederetur,: prioribus comitiis,: priore anno,the year before,; ; : prioris anni consules,; : Dionysius prior,the elder,: vinum,of last year,: priore libro,in the previous book,: pedes,the forefeet,; : canities homini semper a priori parte capitis, tum deinde ab aversā,the forepart,.—Pleon.: cum prior Romanus exercitus praevenisset,: prius praecepta res erat,; cf. .— Old neutr. prior: hoc senatusconsultum prior factum est, Val. Antias ap. P.: prior bellum, Quadrig. ib.: foedus prior, (cf.: bellum Punicum posterior, Cass. Hem. ib.).—
Former, i. e. deceased (late Lat.): inter prieres fratres,.—
Subst.: prĭōres, um, m., forefathers, ancestors, the ancients (poet. and in post-Aug. prose): abiturus illuc, quo priores abierunt,: nomen dixere priores Ortygiam,: nec ingeniis investigata priorum,; : priores tradiderunt,: nostri,: more priorum,; .—
Trop., better, superior, preferable, more excellent or important (not in Cic. and Cæs.): bellante prior,: color puniceae flore prior rosae,; : ut nemo haberetur prior,: aetate et sapientiā,: consilio et manu,: neque prius, neque antiquius quidquam habuit, quam, etc.,.—Esp. with potior: potius quanto prius potiusque est Philippum nobis conjungere quam hos,: nulla (res) prior potiorque visa est,: nihil prius nec potius visum,: unus Plinius est mihi priores, i. e. worth more than they all, Sent. Augur. ap. : artium multitudine prior omnibus, eloquentiā nulli secundus,.—Hence, adv. comp.: prĭus.
Before, sooner, first, previously (class.).
Alone: quem fuit aequius, ut prius introieram in vitam, sic prius exire de vitā,: regem prius Europā, post et Asiā, expellere,: ut vos prius experti estis, nunc Antiochus experitur,; so, prius ... nunc,: prius ... tum,; : prius .... postea,.—
With quam, and often joined in one word, priusquam.
Before that, before: prius quam lucet, assunt,before dawn,: prius illi erimus quam tu,: prius quam plane aspexit ilico eum esse dixit,: nihil prius mihi faciendum putavi, quam ut, etc.,: cui prius quam de ceteris rebus respondeo, de amicitiā pauca dicam,before,: quod ego, prius quam loqui coepisti, sensi,: neque prius fugere destiterunt, quam ad flumen Rhenum pervenerunt,: quid potius faciam, prius quam me dormitum conferam, non reperio,: priusquam aggrediar, etc.,: prius quam ad portam venias,.—
Sooner, rather: Aegyptii quamvis carnificinam prius subierint, quam ibin aut aspidem violent,; ; .—Sometimes in an inverted order: ad hoc genus hominum duravi, quam prius me ad plures penetravi,; (3, 10, 10); v. Zumpt, Gram. § 576.—
In gen., formerly, in former times (poet.), : sed haec prius fuere: nunc, etc.,; .

la:adv:pridie.html:
prīdĭē, adv.
from the obsol. pri (whence prior, primus, pridem) and dies
.
Lit., on the day before (class.; opp. postridie).— Constr. absol., with acc. of the day from which the reckoning was made, or with quam (class.); also, with gen. (class. only in the phrase pridie ejus diei).
Absol., : cui cum pridie frequentes essetis assensi, postridie ad spem estis inanem pacis devoluti,: postero die tropaeum posuit, quo loco pridie pugnatum est,: pridie asservata materia,.—
With quam: si hic pridie natus foret, quam hic est,: pridie quam ego Athenas veni,: haec epistula est pridie data quam illa,.—
With gen.: pridie ejus diei,on the day before this day, the day before,: insidiarum,the day before the ambush,: Kalendarum,.—
With acc., designating the day (v. Madvig. § 230, obs. 1): pridie Idus,: Compitalia,: Quinquatrus,: eum diem,: Parilia,: Circenses,: constitutam diem,: nuptiarum diem, Fest. s. v. Regillis, p. 286 Müll.: vindemias,: aequinoctium autumnale,.—
Transf., the phrase pridie Kalendas (Nonas, etc.) is used as a subst.: nos in Formiano esse volumus usque ad pridie Nonas Maias,: ex ante diem III. Non. Jun. usque ad prid. Kal. Sept.,: gignit id maxime arcturi exortus ex a. d. pridie Idus Septembris,; cf.: EX. A. D. V. KAL. DEC. AD PR. KAL. JAN. SEXT., for six years, to the 31st December, : litterarum datarum pridie Kal. Januar. suavem habuit recordationem clarissimi jurisjurandi, the 31st of December, .—With an acc., not designating a day: quod uxorem pridie sortitionem ductam postridie repudiasset, Roth (Oud. sortitione).—
In gen., before, a short time before (post-class.), ; : Psyche, non ita, ut pridie, parvula,.

In gen.: origo principii nulla est: nam ex principio oriuntur omnia,: quid est cujus principium aliquod sit, nihil sit extremum?: nec principium, nec finem habere,: cujus criminis neque principium invenire, neque evolvere exitum possum,: hic fons, hoc principium est movendi,: bellorum atque imperiorum,: principium pontis,: principio lucis,at daybreak,: in principiis dicendi,at the commencement of a speech,; so of a declaration in a lawsuit,: suave quoddam principium dicendi,: principia ducere ab aliquo, to derive, deduce: omnium rerum magnarum principia a dis immortalibus ducuntur,: principium urbis,: scribendi recte sapere est et principium et fons,: omne principium huc refer,: a Jove principium,: anni,: a sanguine Teucri Ducere principium,: capessere,to begin,.—Adverb.: principio, a principio, in principio, at or in the beginning, at first: principio ... postea, etc.,: principio generi animantium omni est a naturā tributum, ut se tueatur,; ; ; ; ; ; ; so, a principio: ac vellem a principio te audissem, etc.,: dixeram a principio, de re publicā ut sileremus,: in principio,: principio ut,as soon as,; v. Ritschl ad h. l.— Rarely of the boundaries of a country or people: adusque principia Carmanorum,.—
In partic.
Plur., beginnings, foundations, principles, elements (class.): bene provisa et diligenter explorata principia ponantur,: juris,: naturae,; for which: principia naturalia,; cf. : principia rerum, ex quibus omnia constant,first principles, elements,.— Prov.: obsta principiis (cf. the French: ce n'est que le premier pas qui coute),.—
That makes a beginning, that votes first: tribus principium fuit, pro tribu Q. Fabius primus scivit, Lex Thoria, Rudorff. p. 142; Lex Appar. ap. Haubold, Moment. Leg. p. 85; Plebissc. ap. : Faucia curia fuit principium,was the first to vote,—
In gen., a beginner, originator, founder, ancestor (poet.): Graecia principium moris fuit,: mihi Belus avorum Principium,ancestor, progenitor,.—Here, too, prob. belongs PRINCIPIA SACRA, Æneas and

his successors in Lavinium, ancestors whom the Latins and Romans honored as deities, .—

In milit. lang.: princĭpĭa, ōrum, n.
The foremost ranks, the front line of soldiers, the front or van of an army: post principia,behind the front,; cf.: hic ero post principia, inde omnibus signum dabo,: post principia paulatim recedunt, Sisenn. ap. : deinde ipse paulatim procedere; Marium post principia habere,: traversis principiis, in planum deducit,: equites post principia collocat,; . —
The staff-officers, members of the council of war (post-class.): mittere principia,: a principiis salutari,: advocatis legionum principiis et turmarum,; Cod. 12, 47, 1.—
A large open space in a camp, in which were the tents of the general, lieutenants, and tribunes, together with the standards, and where speeches were made and councils held; the general's quarters: jura reddere in principiis,: in principiis ac praetorio in unum sermones confundi,: castrorum,: in castris,: in principiis statuit tabernaculum, eoque omnes cotidie convenire (jussit), ut ibi de summis rebus consilia caperentur,; ; ; : primores centurionum et paucos militum in principia vocat,; ; ; cf. .—
Precedence, preference, the first place: principium ergo, columenque omnium rerum preti margaritae tenent,. —
Plur., selections, selected passages: principiorum libri circumferuntur, quia existimatur pars aliqua etiam sine ceteris esse perfecta,.—
In partic., mastery, dominion (post-class.): ἀρχή, magisterium, magistratus, praesidatus, principium, Gloss. Philox.: in Graeco principii vocabulum, quod est ἀρχή, non tantum ordinativum, sed et potestativum capit principatum, .

la:adv:pridem.html:
prīdem, adv.
from the obsol. pri-, prei-, (= prae; whence prior, primus, pridie), with demonstrative suffix dem
,
long ago, long since, a long time ago; without a negative: ita me pridem facere atriensem voluerat,; : quod ad me pridem scripseras,; .—With a negative: non pridem, haud pridem, not long ago, a short time ago, lately (class.): hoc ego mali non pridem inveni,: recens natura est mundi, neque pridem exordia cepit,: haud ita pridem,not so very long ago,: Themistocles fuit, nostrā civitate non ita pridem dominatu regio liberatā,not long before,.—In old times, in former times, in time past, aforetime, formerly: nunc jam non classem, in quam, sicuti pridem, confugiant, superesse,: Italiam notiorem sibi nunc, quam pridem fuisse,: eodem igitur furore in paenitentiam, quo pridem in iram versus, mori voluit,: quam pridem, how long ago, for how long a time: quam pridem pater et mater mortui essent,: quam pridem non edisti,; ; .

princĭpātus, ūs, m.
princeps
,
the first place, pre-eminence, preference (class.).
In gen.: omnem naturam necesse est .. habere aliquem in se principatum, ut in homine mentem ... in arborum autem radicibus inesse principatus putatur. Principatum autem id dico, quod Graeci ἡγεμονικόν vocant, quo nihil in quoque genere nec potest, nec debet esse praestantius, : animi,: ut quisque aetate antecedit, ita sententiae principatum tenet,: Gallia hujus belli sustinendi principatum tenet, i. e. in bello sustinendo,: eloquentiae dignitatis principatum dare,: qui tibi detulerat ex latronibus suis principatum,: sol astrorum obtinet principatum, id. N. D. 2, 19, 49: principatum in oleo obtinuit Italia,; ; .—
In partic.
The chief place in the state or the army, the post of commander-in-chief: Cassio dominatum et principatum dari,: Cingetorigi principatus atque imperium est traditum,: obtinere principatum totius Galliae,: se dejectos principatu,: de principatu contendere,.—
Of the empire (post-Aug.), reign, empire, dominion, sovereignty: Nero toto principatu suo hostis generis humani,: Fenestella, qui obiit novissimo Tiberii Caesaris principatu,: Nerva res olim dissociabiles miscuit, principatum et libertatem,; ; ; ; .—
A beginning, origin (class. but very rare): an mundus ab aliquo temporis principatu ortus est?; cf.: totius opusculi principatus,the beginning, P.—
The hosts of angels, good or bad (eccl. Lat.), ; .

princĭpor, āri,

la:adj:princeps.html:
princeps, cĭpis, adj. and
subst. comm. [primus-capio], first in time or order (syn. primus).—Lit., in gen.: ut quisque in fugā postremus, ita periculo princeps erat,: princeps in proelium ibat, ultimus conserto proelio excedebat,: princeps Horatius ibat,first, in front, in advance, Weissenb. ad

loc.: princeps fuit ad conatum exercitus comparandi,: Firmani principes pecuniae pollicendae fuerunt,were the first to promise,: princeps in agendo,; : omnium nationum exterarum princeps Sicilia se ad amicitiam populi Romani applicuit,was the first that entered into friendship with the Roman people,: princeps et solus bellum his indixit,: princeps in haec verba jurat,: ut principes talem nuntium attulisse viderentur,to be the first,: qui Formiarum moenia dicitur Princeps tenuisse,: matri Qui dederit princeps oscula,: princeps turmas inducit Asilas,: princeps ante omnes,first of all,.—Of things: quoniam exordium princeps omnium esse debet,: qualitatum aliae sunt principes, aliae ex lis ortae,original,: mensis Romani anni,: addere principi Limo particulam,: dies imperii princeps, vitae supremus,.—

The first, chief, the most eminent, distinguished, or noble (syn. primores): longe omnium gravitate princeps Plato,: Eudoxus in astrologiā facile princeps,: quaedam principes feminae,certain noble ladies,: principe loco genitus,.—Prov.: principibus placuisse viris non ultima laus est,. —Rarely of things: gemma princeps Sardonychus,.—
As subst.: princeps, cĭpis, m., the first man, first person: princeps senatŭs,the first senator on the censor's list, the first member of the Senate,.—
Esp., the first, chief, principal, most distinguished person: quales in re publicā principes essent, talis reliquos solere esse civis,: juventutis,one of the noblest of the Roman knights,: trecenti conjuravimus principes juventutis Romanae, i. e. high-born or patrician youths, (= proceres juventutis, ); 42, 61, 5.—In the time of the emperors this was also a title of honor given to the prince, the heir to the empire, : sacerdotum,the high-priest,. —
A chief, head, author, originator, leader, contriver, etc.: princeps atque architectus sceleris,: Zeno eorum (Stoicorum) princeps non tam rerum inventor fuit, quam verborum novorum,: princeps Argonautarum,i. e. Jason,: principes consilii publici, i. e. senatus,: conjurationis,: eorum omnium hic dux est atque princeps,: regendae civitatis dux et sententiae princeps in senatu,: (pueri) aequalium principes,first among their playfellows,: gregis,i. e. of players,: principes sententiarum consulares,who were first asked for their opinion,: hujus consilii principes,: belli inferendi,first in commencing hostilities,: jam princeps equitum,at the head of,.—Of ancestors: hinc Dardanus ortus Iasiusque pater, genus a quo principe nostrum, (cf., in this sense, principium, ; v. principium, II. B. 2.).—
A chief, superior, director (ante- and post-class.): principes, qui utrique rei praeponuntur,; .—
A prince, i. e. a ruler, sovereign, emperor (poet. and post-Aug.): hic ames dici pater atque princeps,; ; : quae non faciet quod principis uxor,; .—
In milit. lang.: princĭpes, um, m., the second line of soldiers, between the hastati and triarii, ; ; ; 37, 39; cf. ; ; ; cf. ; and Becker, Antiq. 3, 2, p. 249 sq.; p. 269 sq.—Princeps also signifies,
A company or division of the principes: signum primi principis, of the first company of the principes, : octavum principem duxit,was centurion of the eighth maniple,.—
A centurion or captain of the principes: princeps prior, the first captain of the principes, : princeps tertiae legionis,; cf. .—
The office of centurion of the principes, the centurionship or captaincy of the principes: mihi primus princeps prioris centuriae est adsignatus, the first captaincy of the principes, .—Comp.: omnium priorum principum principiorem, si dici fas est,.

la:adv:privatim.html:
prīvātim, adv.
id.
.
In gen., apart from State affairs, for one's self, as an individual, in private, privately, in a private capacity (opp. publice; class.): eloquentiā et privatim et publice homines perverse abutuntur,: aut privatim gerere aliquid malunt, aut capessunt rem publicam,: privatim mandare rem alicui,: in peregrino quaeritur, privatimne an publice venerit,: nec societatem tibi quippiam debere nec privatim

Quintium debuisse, : privatim degeneres, in publicum exitiosi,: privatim et publice rapere vasa caelata,: publice privatimque gratiam petere,: fidem sanctam habuit tam privatim, quam publice,towards individuals,; opp. publicitus,: qui privatim plus possint quam ipsi magistratus,: nulla me ipsum privatim pepulit insignis injuria,; : Fabius infestus privatim Papirio erat,personally,.—

In partic.
Apart, separately, especially, particularly (post-Aug.): de iis privatim condidit volumen Amometus,: oleum cicinum privatim dicitur purgare praecordia,: appellatione privatim sibi assignatā,.—
At home: nec privatim se tenuit, in foro inambulavit,.

la:noun:privignus.html:
prīvignus, i, m., and prīvigna, ae, f.

.
A step-son; a step-daughter (class.): uxor liberis ex aliā uxore natis noverca dicitur: matris vir ex alio viro natis vitricus appellatur: eorum uterque natos aliunde privignos privignasque vocant,.
Privignus, ; ; ; ; ; : PRIVIGNVS MEVS, Monum. Ancyr.: venenum privigno datum,.—
Privigna: de uxore Tuberonis et privignā,; .—
Plur.: illic matre carentibus Privignis mulier temperat innocens,step-children,; .—
Transf., of plants (poet.), adj.: privignae proles,.

la:adj:pristinus.html:
pristĭnus, a, um, adj.
cf. priscus
,
former, early, original, primitive, pristine (class.): tua pristina dignitas et gloria,, b, 2: labor meus pristinus,: vestra pristina bonitas et misericordia,: veterem consuetudinem fori et pristinum morem judiciorum requirere,: odio pristino incensa mulier,: pristinum animum erga populum Romanum conservare,: pro pristina amicitiā,: reminiscens pristini temporis,: consuetudo,: pristina omnium confirmatur opinio,: in pristinum statum redire,; so, gloria,: conjux,: mens,: consulatus super pristinum quattuor gessit,: annotationes, Gell. praef.: pristina jura recipere,.—Subst.: pristĭ-num, i, n., a former condition: in pristinum restituere,.—
In partic.
Just past, preceding, previous, of yesterday: diei pristini perfidia,: somnium pristinae noctis,.—
= priscus, old-fashioned, old, former, early (ante-class. and postAug.): in vobis resident mores pristini,: tribus pristinum nomen possident,: aetas,.

one of the first, of the first rank, chief, principal, excellent, remarkable (class.): primarius parasitus,: quoad primarius vir dicat,the first speaker, he who has a right to be heard,: primarius vir populi,: femina,: bellator,, 43, 45, § 139.—Of things: condicio,: non ea, quae primario loco sunt, sed ea, quae secundum locum obtinent, dub. la:other:Primus.html:
prīmus, a, um,
adj. sup. [obsol. prep. pri (prei); whence also prior, priscus; cf.: privus, privo, etc., and v. pro], the first, first (properly only when three or more are referred to. The first, as opp. to the second, is prior; but primus is rarely used for prior,).
In gen.: qui primus vulnus dicitur obligavisse,: primus sentio mala nostra: primus rescisco omnia: Primus porro obnuntio,: verum primum: verum igitur et extremum,: primae litterae,: primus inter homines nobilissimos,: primi ex omnibus philosophis,: primus Graeciae in Thraciam introiit,: primus de mille fuisses,: in primis,among the first, in the foremost ranks,: in primis stetit,: in primis pugnantes,: leonem primus, aut in primis ferire, : utque pedum primis infans vestigia plantis institerat (= ut primum, etc., poet.), : primus post eos quos poëtae tradiderunt movisse aliqua circa rhetoricen Empedocles dicitur (= secundus or proximus ab iis),.—
In partic.
In time or place, first, fore, foremost, the first part; sometimes to be translated, the end, extremity, etc.: in primā provinciā,at the entrance of the province,: digitus,the tip of the finger,: dentes,the front teeth,: ranis prima lingua cohaeret,the end of the tongue,: primā statim nocte,at the beginning of the night,: sol,i. e. the rising sun,: luna,i. e. the new moon,.—With quisque, the first possible, the very first: primo quoque tempore,at the very first opportunity,: primo quoque die,: me tibi primum quidque concedente,: fluit voluptas et prima quaeque avolat,.—Subst.: prīma, ōrum, n., the first part, the beginning: quod bellum, si prima satis prospera fuissent,.—Of the first principles or elements of things, : prima consiliorum (for prima consilia),: a primo, from the beginning, at first: multum improbiores sunt quam a primo credidi,; ; : in illā pro Ctesiphonte oratione submissius a primo: deinde pressius,: suam vim retinere a primo ad extremum,: hoc a primo cogitavit,; Halm ad loc.: id a primo rectissime dicitur, Madv. ad loc.: in primo, in front, before, in the beginning, first: equites in primo late ire jubet,in the van,: qui numerus in primo viget, jacet in extremo,. —
First in rank or station, chief, principal, most excellent, eminent, distinguished, noble (cf.: princeps, primores): evocat ad se Massiliensium quindecim primos,: sui municipii facile primus,: homo,: primis urbis placuisse,: juvenum primi,: est genus hominum, qui esse primos se omnium rerum volunt Nec sunt,: quia sum apud te primus,I am the first in your favor,: primus humani generis,: urbem Italiae primam,: praedium,: suavia prima habere,to give the first place to, think the most of,: otium atque divitiae, quae prima mortales putant,: cura,a chief part,.—Also, most conspicuous, chief, in a bad sense: peccatores, quorum primus ego sum,: primas partes, or primas agere,to play the first part, to occupy the first rank,: primas in causis agebat Hortensius,; : primas dare, to give the first place, ascribe the greatest importance to a thing: actioni primas dedisse Demosthenes dicitur, cum rogaretur, quid in dicendo esset primum: huic secundas, huic tertias,: primas deferre, to transfer the first or principal part: amoris erga me tibi primas defero,i. e. I assign to you the first rank among those who love me,: primas concedere, to yield the first place: si Allienus tibi primas in dicendo partes concesserit,: primas tenere,to play the first part, be the best,: cum primis, and in primis (also written in one word, impri-mis), with or among the first, chiefly, especially, principally, particularly: homo domi suae cum primis locuples,: in primis lautus eques,: oppidum in primis Siciliae clarum,: homo in primis improbissimus,, § 68: vir magnus in primis,: in primis hoc a se animadversum esse dicebat,: in primis nobis sermo de te fuit,: in primis ... dein,first, in the first place,. —Hence, adv., primo and primum; also, ante- and post-class. and very rare, prime and primiter (the form primo is usually limited to that which is strictly first in time; primum in enumerations of contemporary facts, things, or arguments, where the order is at the speaker's choice; cf. Krebs, Antibarb. p. 920 sq.).
prīmō, at first, at the beginning, first, firstly.
In gen.: aedes primo ruere rebamur,: neque credebam primo mihimet Sosiae,; : primo non accredidit,: Themistocles solus primo profectus est,: contemptus est primo a tyrannis,; .—
With dein, deinde, inde, post, postea, mox, denique, nunc: primo Stoicorum more agamus, deinde nostro instituto vagabimur,: primo pecuniae, dein imperii cupido crevit,: primo ... deinde ... tum ... tum,: primo ... deinde,; ; ; : primo abstinentiā utendum: deinde danda, etc.,: primo ... inde, ... hinc,: haec primo paulatim crescere: post, etc.,: dissuadente primo Vercingetorige, post concedente,: primo ... postea ... postremo, etc.,: primo ... mox,: primo ... mox deinde,: primo negitare, denique saepius fatigatus, etc.,: neque illi credebam primo, nunc vero palam est,.—
(Mostly post-Aug. for primum.) With iterum, rursus, secundo: primo ... iterum,: primo ... rursus,: primo ... secundo,.—
prīmum, at first, first, in the first place, in the beginning (class.).
In enumerations, with a foll. deinde, tum: Caesar primum suo, deinde omnium e conspectu remotis equis,: primum ... deinde ... deinde,: primum ... deinde ... tum ... postremo,: primum ... deinde ... praeterea ... postremo,: primum ... tum ... deinde ... post ... tum ... deinde ....,; ; cf.: primum ... secundo loco ... deinde ... tum,; ; ; ; ; ; : primum ... subinde,: primum ... mox,.—
Without other adverbs.
In gen.: quaerenda pecunia primum est,: te Quicumque primum Produxit,; .—
Strengthened with omnium, first of all, : primum omnium ego ipse vigilo,.—
With ut, ubi, simulac, cum.
Ut primum, ubi primum, simul ac primum, cum primum, as soon as ever, as soon as: ut primum potestas data est augendae dignitatis tuae, etc.,: ubi primum potuit, istum reliquit,: simul ac primum niti possunt, etc.,: tum affuerat, cum primum dati sunt judices,.—
Nunc primum, now first, now for the first time (cf.: nunc demum, now at last): post illa nunc primum audio, Quid illo sit factum,.—
With dum (also by Plaut. joined in one word, pri-mumdum), in the first place, first (anteclass.): primum dum, si falso insimulas, etc. Iterum si id verum est, etc.,: omnium primumdum haed aedes jam face occlusae sicut,; ; : primum dum omnium male dictitatur tibi vulgo in sermonibus,.—
With adv. or other expression of time, for the first time: hodie primum ire in ganeum,: quo die primum convocati su mus,.—*
prīmē, es pecially: fabula prime proba, Naev. ap. P.; cf. P.—
prīmĭter, at first, first of all (ante- and post-class.): eripis primiter dapes, Pompon. ap. ; Inscr. (of the beginning of the third century of Christ) Lab. Epigr. Lat. Scop. in Egitto.

Prĭămus, i, m., = Πρίαμος.

(Ann. v. 17 Vahl.): o pater, o patria, o Pria. mi domus! id. ap. (Trag v. 118 Vahl.); ; ; cf. ; ; ; and 90.—

la:adj:priscus.html:
priscus, a, um, adj.
for prius-cus, like pris-tinus for prius-tinus, and magis for magius, a comparative form
,
of or belonging to former times, of many years ago, old, olden, ancient, primitive, antique. Like the Greek ἀρχαῖος, it denotes that which existed before our time, while pristinus is applied also to those things which have existed in our day (class.; cf.: vetus, antiquus).

Former, previous (poet.): quid si prisca redit Venus?: nomen,; .—

With abl.: haec meretrix meum erum ... privavit bonis, luce, honore,: donis privatus sum,: aliquem approbatione,: praepositio in privat verbum eā vi, quam haberet, si in praepositum non fuisset,: aliquem somno,: se oculis,: aliquem vitā,: aliquem communi luce,: patriam aspectu suo,: cibo,: lumine,: fide,.—

To free, release, deliver from any thing; with abl.: aliquem injuriā,: exsilio,: molestiā,: dolore,: dolore,: dominis superbis,: formidine,.—Hence,
prīvantĭa, ĭum, n., privatives, a transl. of the Gr. στερητικά: sunt enim alia contraria, quae privantia licet appellemus Latine, Graece appellantur στερητικά, .—
prīvātus, a, um, P. a.
Apart from the State, peculiar to one's self, of or belonging to an individual, private (opp. publicus or communis; cf. domesticus; class.): nihil privati ac separati agri,: utatur privatis ut suis,: privatus illis census erat brevis, Commune magnum,: vestem mutare privato consensu, opp. publico consilio,: de communi quicquid poterat, ad se in privatam domum sevocabat,: res quae ipsius erant privatae,private property,: privatae feriae vocantur sacrorum propriorum, velut dies natales, Müll.—
Esp., of persons, not in public or official life, private, deprived of office: cum projectis fascibus et deposito imperio, privatus et captus ipse in alienam venisset potestatem,; : vir privatus, a private individual, one who is not a magistrate, or in any public office: privato viro imperium extra ordinem dare,: Bibulus ex iis, qui privati sunt,: privatus an cum potestate,: privati, opp. reges,.—
Of things: aedificia,isolated, apart from the villages,: vita privata et quieta,a private life, withdrawn from State affairs,.—
Neutr. absol. in the phrases in privato, in private, opp. in publico, in public, : in privatum, for private use: tabernas vendidit in privatum,: ex privato, from one's private property: tributum ex privato conferre,.—

Fragm. ap. P.
